strengths: Formulates single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point-trajectory grids and uses latent flow matching with a VAE, adapting video-generator-style architectures to motion trajectories.

Strong empirical results across multiple datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101), outperforming regression-based trackers (ATM, Tra-MoE), generative trajectory methods (Track2Act), and several video generators on multiple metrics.
Controlled modality ablation (RGB vs. trajectory latents) provides evidence for the central hypothesis that pixel generation overhead harms motion plausibility and efficiency.
Highly efficient compared to video generators: much smaller models and faster inference, with detailed reporting of compute and hyperparameters.
Reproducibility is generally strong: architecture, training details, hyperparameters, evaluation cost, and limitations are discussed in the appendix.
User study and physical-plausibility metric (LRTL) complement standard distributional metrics and support the method's advantages.
Ethical considerations and broader impact, as well as limitations, are explicitly addressed.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: direct trajectory prediction, flow matching, and dense point tracking are existing ideas; the contribution is mainly a well-executed combination and an empirical finding rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

Evaluation inconsistencies are concerning: for the same models, FVMD/LRTL numbers differ dramatically between Table 11 and Tables 3/12 (e.g., Ours(L) FVMD 6470 vs. 13745), with no explanation, which undermines reproducibility and confidence in the reported results.

The real-world Physics101 main result seems to use the no-VAE variant, while the method is presented with VAE; the appendix shows the VAE variant performs worse overall (31.67 vs. 28.62), so the claim that 'our method outperforms WAN overall' is not supported for the full proposed method.

Comparison with video generators may be unfair: billion-parameter models are fine-tuned for roughly the same wall-clock time as training the proposed small model from scratch; WAN 14B is not fine-tuned at all; and reliance on CoTracker to extract motion may compound tracking errors, especially on generated videos with poor motion.
Metrics have known limitations: FVMD is marginal and may miss per-image plausibility; LRTL is minimized by static predictions; and the user study involves only 20 users and 16 scenes.

Baselines ATM and Tra-MoE are evaluated with MSE against pseudo-ground-truth from CoTracker, differing from their original success-rate/trajectory-conditioning objectives; fairness of the text-conditioning and point-filtering protocol could be questioned.

The claim that dense grid prediction captures scene-wide context is not directly ablated against sparse variants with the same generative architecture, so the source of improvement is not fully isolated.
Real-world validation is limited to small-scale experiments; the method is not demonstrated at in-the-wild scale, and generalization remains limited as acknowledged.

strengths: Formulates single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point-trajectory grids, which is a reasonable and somewhat promising framing.

Uses flow matching in a learned trajectory latent space and adapts a video-generator-style transformer architecture, yielding an efficient model at inference time compared with large video generators.
Evaluates on multiple synthetic and real datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101) and includes distributional, physical-plausibility, and user-study evaluations.
The dense grid formulation may better capture scene-wide context than sparse active-point regression methods, and the paper attempts to directly compare against both trajectory and video baselines.
Provides substantial implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute estimates, which partially supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method largely composes existing ingredients (point trajectories, VAE latent modeling, flow matching, transformer blocks adapted from video generation). The core idea of generating point trajectories is already present in prior work such as Track2Act; the dense-grid and latent-flow-matching variants are incremental rather than a fundamental advance.

The central claim that video generators fail mainly because of the overhead of generating RGB pixels is not convincingly established. Comparisons to video generators are confounded by fine-tuning duration, model capacity, resolution/aspect-ratio preprocessing, CoTracker extraction errors on generated videos, and the use of different training objectives. CoTracker accuracy is verified only on ground-truth videos, not on generated videos, so motion errors may partly reflect tracking failures rather than purely pixel-generation overhead.

Evaluation metrics have serious weaknesses. Best-of-K MSE rewards sampling diversity and can be gamed; FVMD and FVMD(S) are not fully justified or described for trajectory distributions; LRTL is minimized by static predictions and thus cannot stand alone as a physical-plausibility metric. No statistical significance, variance, or confidence intervals are reported.

The paper contains major numerical inconsistencies. For example, for the same Kubric in-distribution setting, Ours(L) has FVMD/LRTL 13745/14.1 in Table 3, but Ours(L) has 6470/6.4 in Table 11 and 13745/14.6 in Table 12; Ours(B) also differs drastically between Table 11 and Table 12. Table 4 reports out-of-distribution FVMD lower than in-distribution for Ours(L), contradicting the stated trend. Table 8 and Table 14 imply the main Physics101 result may correspond to a no-VAE variant, despite VAE being part of the method. These inconsistencies substantially undermine trust in the reported results.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently fair. ATM and Tra-MoE are active-point policy-conditioned models, not direct dense motion-forecasting baselines, and are evaluated with filtered/selected points favorable to them but still not matched to the generative setting. Track2Act is heavily modified (goal dropped, horizon extended, point count changed), and MotionModes is adapted with ground-truth masks, so the comparisons may not reflect the published methods' actual capabilities.

Real-world evaluation is weak: Physics101 uses only one sample per model per initial condition and a single CoTracker pseudo-ground-truth, with a modest overall improvement (28.62 vs 30.08), while Physion real-world results are purely qualitative. There is no downstream task evaluation showing the predicted trajectories are useful for control, planning, or physical reasoning.

The physical problem is ill-posed from a single image; the method predicts only 2D point tracks and does not explicitly model 3D state, object properties, forces, or camera motion. In camera-mounted settings such as LIBERO effector views, camera and object motion may be confounded, making the forecasting objective ambiguous.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release or checkpoints are mentioned, and although appendix hyperparameters are given, several architectural and metric details (e.g., exact FVMD(S) computation, Best-of-K matching, LRTL normalization) remain unclear. The reported evaluation compute is very large, making independent reproduction difficult.

Writing and notation are not sufficiently clear for a top-tier venue. There are inconsistent symbols (r, r1, r2, H/r vs H/r2, W/r vs W/r1), placeholder or malformed references, typos, and table/header issues. Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

The user study is small (20 users, 16 scenes) and lacks details on statistical significance, user demographics, or whether rankings are robust. Ethical concerns are mentioned but not deeply addressed, particularly regarding surveillance and behavioral prediction misuse.

strengths: Formulates single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point trajectory grids, effectively modeling uncertainty and scene-wide context rather than regressing sparse points or generating RGB pixels.

Strong empirical results across several benchmarks: outperforms regression-based trajectory forecasters (ATM, Tra-MoE), diffusion-based trajectory generator (Track2Act), a training-free motion method (MotionModes), and adapted state-of-the-art video generators on Kubric, LIBERO, and Physics101.

The controlled modality ablation is compelling: holding the architecture and latent dimensionality comparable, trajectory generation produces substantially better motion accuracy and rigidity than RGB generation, directly supporting the paper's central hypothesis about the overhead of pixel generation.

Evaluation is thorough and multi-faceted, including Best-of-K MSE, FVMD, image-wise FVMD, the LRTL rigidity metric, metric validation, a user study, and qualitative real-world generalization from synthetic training.

Addresses a timely and important question about whether video generators are effective world models for motion forecasting, showing that even fine-tuned large video models struggle on simple physical scenarios while a smaller trajectory generator performs better.
Reproducibility is generally strong: extensive appendix with architecture details, training hyperparameters, hardware requirements, sampling procedures, evaluation cost, and user-study protocol.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation remains limited: Physics101 results are mixed and rely on a single pseudo-ground-truth per condition, while real-world generalization from Physion is only qualitative. This weakens broad in-the-wild claims.

Comparison with video generators may be affected by adaptation choices such as trajectory extraction via CoTracker, fine-tuning duration, and resolution/padding. Although the paper controls many variables, it does not fully rule out that larger-scale video pretraining or longer fine-tuning could improve motion forecasting.

The VAE ablation is inconsistent: latent trajectory modeling helps on Kubric and LIBERO but hurts on Physics101. The paper de-emphasizes this mixed result; a clearer account of when and why latent modeling is beneficial would strengthen the method.

Some metrics have acknowledged limitations (e.g., LRTL is minimized by no motion, FVMD measures marginal rather than conditional distributions), and evaluation is largely confined to simulated environments or pseudo-tracked real data.

Novelty is mainly in task formulation and adaptation of modern generative architectures to the trajectory modality, rather than a fundamentally new generative mechanism; the contribution is empirically strong but methodologically incremental.

strengths: Introduces a novel formulation of image-based motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense point trajectory grids, using a latent flow-matching model inspired by video generators. This naturally models uncertainty and scene-wide motion.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation across synthetic and real datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101, Cityscapes) and a wide range of baselines, including regression-based trajectory predictors (ATM, Tra-MoE), generative trajectory methods (Track2Act), and large pretrained video generators (WAN, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter).

Strong evidence that direct trajectory generation outperforms regression and sparse-point forecasting, and that dense grid-based modeling improves motion accuracy and physical consistency over active-point methods.

Includes a useful modality ablation showing that switching from RGB generation to trajectory generation substantially improves motion quality, supporting the paper's central hypothesis about pixel-generation overhead.
Well-written and well-organized, with extensive implementation details, reproducibility information, compute requirements, user study details, limitations, and an ethics statement.
Demonstrates promising efficiency gains: the trajectory model is orders of magnitude faster and smaller at inference than large video generators, while producing more plausible motion.
weaknesses: Several quantitative results are inconsistent or unexplained. For example, FVMD/LRTL values for Ours (B/L) in Table 13 and Table 17 differ by orders of magnitude from the main Kubric results in Tables 3, 4, and 14, without sufficient explanation of different protocols or metric scales.

The claim that video generators fail mainly because of RGB pixel overhead is not fully isolated. The baselines differ in architecture, latent space, pretraining, fine-tuning, and tracking-based evaluation, so alternative explanations (e.g., domain mismatch, limited fine-tuning, sampling/tracking errors) are not completely ruled out.

Real-world evaluation is less conclusive. On Physics101, the overall improvement over WAN is small and the method is worse in 2/5 scenarios; the VAE ablation on real data is ambiguous or worse with VAE. Cityscapes uses pseudo ground truth from CoTracker and only one future per clip, limiting distributional evaluation.

The LRTL rigidity metric is an indirect proxy for physical plausibility. It assumes low-rank trajectory structure and may penalize legitimate non-rigid or articulated motion, so it does not fully establish physical consistency.

The user study is relatively small (20 users, 16 scenes), and some qualitative claims rely on appendix results with unexplained metric scales. Broader generalization remains limited, as the authors acknowledge.

Novelty is meaningful but incremental relative to prior trajectory-generation, VAE-based motion forecasting, and video-generation-as-world-model work; the main new element is the combination of dense trajectory generation with latent flow matching and the systematic comparison to video generators.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated formulation of single-image motion forecasting as conditional generation of dense point-trajectory grids, explicitly modeling uncertainty and scene-wide context rather than only sparse active points.

Sensible architecture: latent VAE for trajectories plus rectified flow/flow matching, with DINOv2 image conditioning and a spatio-temporal transformer; implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute are documented in the appendix.

Extensive empirical effort across multiple synthetic and real datasets (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101, Cityscapes), with comparisons to regression forecasters, a generative trajectory method, and large-scale video generators.

Interesting and potentially useful analysis of output modality: the RGB-vs-trajectory ablation and joint RGB+trajectory diffusion study attempt to test why video generators may be inefficient at motion forecasting.
Addresses physical plausibility with multiple metrics (FVMD, image-wise FVMD, Best-of-K, LRTL) and includes a user study, plus an ethics statement and limitations section.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core method is a fairly direct combination of existing components—VAE latent modeling, flow matching, video-generator-style transformers, and point tracking/trajectory prediction. The main claimed difference, dense grid generation, is useful but not a deep conceptual advance.

Serious evaluation inconsistencies: FVMD and LRTL values vary dramatically across tables for apparently comparable settings (e.g., Ours(L) FVMD is reported as 13745 in Table 3, 6470 in Table 13, and ~146 in Table 17; LRTL varies from 14.1 to 6.4 to 1.20). These discrepancies are not explained and undermine confidence in the experimental claims.

Baseline comparisons are often unfair or confounded. The stochastic model is frequently compared using Best-of-K / Min with k=8 against deterministic baselines; Best-of-K can strongly favor sampling and is not a clean measure of forecasting quality. Video generators are fine-tuned for the same wall-clock time as much smaller models, and trajectories are extracted with CoTracker, conflating motion quality with tracking errors and RGB artifacts.

Key central claims are overbroad relative to evidence. The conclusion that video generators fail mainly due to RGB-generation overhead is not fully isolated by the architecture-based modality ablation. On out-of-distribution Kubric, the method is sometimes only comparable to fine-tuned video baselines, and Physics101 results are mixed, so the broad critique of video generators as world models is not convincingly established.

Metrics are weak for the claimed task. MSE against a single pseudo ground truth on real data is not suitable for ambiguous multi-modal forecasting; LRTL is acknowledged to be minimized by no motion and is only a proxy for rigidity; user study is small (20 users, 16 questions) with no confidence intervals or significance tests.

Several baselines are adapted in ways that may weaken them (e.g., Track2Act loses goal conditioning, changes horizon and point count; MotionModes addresses a different problem requiring segmentation). The paper does not establish that these are strong, well-tuned baselines under the same information constraints.

Presentation and technical clarity have issues: notation is inconsistent (e.g., r_0, r_s, r), some tables are hard to parse, references appear duplicated/malformed, and several important result tables lack error bars or statistical support.

Ablations are incomplete or inconclusive: the VAE ablation is mixed on real data, sampling-density results use inconsistent metric scales, and there is no clean architecture-matched pixel-vs-trajectory comparison under identical capacity, data, and optimization budgets.

strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated and timely formulation: motion forecasting from a single image as conditional generation of quasi-dense point-trajectory grids, using a video-generator-like latent VAE plus rectified-flow architecture. This is a clear and useful contribution.

It provides broad empirical support across synthetic and real datasets, including Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, and Cityscapes, with comparisons to regression-based trajectory predictors, diffusion-based trajectory generators, and state-of-the-art video generators.

The modality ablation is a particularly strong piece of evidence: holding much of the architecture/training setup fixed, trajectory-latent generation consistently outperforms RGB generation and joint RGB+trajectory generation on several motion-quality metrics, supporting the central claim that pixel generation is an inefficient proxy for motion modeling.

The evaluation is multi-faceted, using distributional metrics, Best-of-K MSE, and a rigidity proxy (LRTL), with additional ablations on sampling density, model scale, VAE use, pseudo-track supervision, and multi-frame conditioning. This makes the main claims more convincing than a single-metric comparison would.

The manuscript is generally clear, includes reproducibility details such as architecture, hyperparameters, training costs, and evaluation protocols, and acknowledges limitations and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: Real-world quantitative evaluation relies heavily on pseudo ground-truth trajectories extracted by CoTracker, and the real-world datasets are relatively small-scale. This weakens claims about broad in-the-wild generalization, even though the qualitative Physion transfer results are promising.

The video-generator comparison may be partially confounded by factors beyond the RGB-vs-trajectory modality, such as resolution/aspect-ratio padding, fine-tuning budget, trajectory extraction from generated videos, and possible tracking failures on unrealistic RGB motion. The paper takes reasonable steps to control these factors, but the conclusion that pixel generation is the primary bottleneck is not fully isolated.

The VAE ablation is not consistently positive: on Physics101 the VAE variant is slightly worse overall than the no-VAE variant. Since latent modeling is a core design choice, a clearer explanation or more extensive real-data ablation would strengthen the method.

The LRTL rigidity metric is a proxy that can be optimized by static or nearly static motion and may not fully capture physical plausibility for non-rigid or deformable objects. While the authors combine it with other metrics, its interpretation requires caution.

Some high-level claims are broader than the evidence, e.g., that video generators struggle to learn basic physical consistency. The experiments are compelling for the selected scenarios, but larger-scale, more diverse physical benchmarks would be needed to support a general conclusion about video world models.

For stochastic trajectory generation, Best-of-K naturally favors methods that can sample multiple hypotheses; the paper also reports MeanT/Mean/Min results, but direct comparison against deterministic baselines remains somewhat asymmetric. The user study is useful but small and limited to two video baselines.
